name: Psalms
author: Psalms is a collection of 150 songs and prayers by many writers over several centuries. The headings credit about half to King David, a shepherd who became Israel's warrior-king and a skilled musician. Others are credited to Asaph and the 'sons of Korah' (families of Levites who led temple music), to King Solomon, and one to Moses, while many carry no name. Many scholars think the headings were added later, and they debate whether the headings always mean authorship, since 'of David' can also mean 'for' or 'in the style of' David.
audience: These songs were first sung by the people of Israel in worship, especially at the temple in Jerusalem, where Levite choirs led with harps, lyres, cymbals and trumpets. Over time the collection became Israel's hymnbook and prayer book, used by pilgrims at festivals, by Jews returning from exile, and later in synagogues.
era: The psalms span many centuries. Tradition traces the oldest to Moses, though many scholars date the earliest to around King David's time, about 1000 BC, when Jerusalem became the capital and Solomon then built the temple. They cover the divided kingdoms, threats from Assyria and Babylon, Jerusalem's destruction in 586 BC and the exile in Babylon. The collection likely reached its final form after the return under Persian rule, when the temple was rebuilt around 516 BC.

notes.1:1: Psalm 1 opens Book One of the five 'books' Psalms is divided into, and many think it was placed first as a doorway into the whole collection.
notes.2:1: Many scholars think this was sung at the crowning of a new king from David's family in Jerusalem.
notes.3:1: The heading links it to the time David fled Jerusalem when his son Absalom led a rebellion to seize the throne.
notes.7:1: The heading links it to words of 'Cush, a Benjaminite', someone from King Saul's tribe, though nothing more is known of him.
notes.9:1: Psalms 9 and 10 may once have been one poem: together they loosely follow the Hebrew alphabet, each section starting with the next letter.
notes.18:1: The heading links it to the day God rescued David from Saul and all his enemies; a nearly identical song appears in 2 Samuel 22.
notes.20:1: A prayer for the king, probably sung at the temple before he led the army out to battle.
notes.21:1: A royal psalm, likely sung at the temple to give thanks for the king, perhaps after a victory.
notes.24:1: Many think it was sung in procession as worshippers, perhaps carrying the ark of the covenant (Israel's sacred chest), approached the temple gates.
notes.30:1: The heading calls it a song for the dedication of 'the house', probably the temple or David's palace in Jerusalem.
notes.34:1: The heading links it to when David, fleeing Saul, pretended to be mad before the Philistine king of Gath (called Abimelech here, Achish in 1 Samuel).
notes.37:1: This is an acrostic: each pair of verses begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, a pattern that may have helped people memorise it.
notes.41:1: This closes Book One of Psalms; the final verse of praise was likely added to mark the end of that collection.
notes.42:1: Opening Book Two, this is the first psalm of the 'sons of Korah', a family of Levite temple singers; Psalms 42 and 43 were probably once one poem.
notes.45:1: A song for a royal wedding, celebrating a king of Israel marrying a foreign princess; which king is unknown.
notes.50:1: The first psalm credited to Asaph, a Levite whom David appointed to lead temple music; his family of singers carried on his name.
notes.51:1: The heading links it to when the prophet Nathan confronted David after his adultery with Bathsheba and the arranged death of her husband Uriah.
notes.52:1: The heading links it to when Doeg the Edomite told Saul that David had visited the priest Ahimelech, which led to the killing of the priests at Nob.
notes.53:1: This is nearly the same as Psalm 14; it seems the song was copied into two different collections that were later joined together.
notes.54:1: The heading links it to when people of Ziph, a town in Judah's wilderness, betrayed David's hiding place to King Saul.
notes.56:1: The heading links it to when the Philistines seized David in Gath, Goliath's hometown, where he had fled from Saul.
notes.57:1: The heading links it to when David hid from Saul in a cave, either the cave of Adullam or one near En Gedi.
notes.59:1: The heading links it to when Saul sent men to watch David's house to kill him, and his wife Michal helped him escape.
notes.60:1: The heading links it to David's wars against the Arameans of Syria, when Joab's army defeated the Edomites in the Valley of Salt.
notes.63:1: The heading places David in the wilderness of Judah, the dry hill country west of the Dead Sea, fleeing either Saul or later Absalom.
notes.70:1: This short psalm is almost identical to the closing verses of Psalm 40.
notes.72:1: The heading credits it to Solomon, David's son; a prayer for the king, it closes Book Two with a note that David's prayers end here.
notes.73:1: Opening Book Three, this begins a group of eleven psalms credited to Asaph and the temple singers who carried on his name.
notes.74:1: It describes the temple burned by enemies, so most think it was written after the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC.
notes.79:1: Like Psalm 74, it mourns Jerusalem in ruins and the temple defiled, most likely after the Babylonian conquest of 586 BC.
notes.80:1: Its mention of Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh leads many to link it to the northern kingdom's collapse under Assyria around 722 BC.
notes.81:1: It was sung at a festival marked by trumpet blasts at the new and full moon, probably the autumn Feast of Tabernacles (Booths).
notes.85:1: Many think it comes from soon after the exiles returned from Babylon, when the land was poor and rebuilding was slow.
notes.88:1: The heading credits it to the sons of Korah and to Heman the Ezrahite. A Heman led temple music in David's day, and a famous wise man of that name is mentioned in Solomon's time, though they may not be the same man.
notes.89:1: Credited to Ethan the Ezrahite, it mourns a defeat of a king from David's line, perhaps Jerusalem's fall; it closes Book Three.
notes.90:1: The heading credits it to Moses, making it traditionally the oldest psalm; it opens Book Four.
notes.92:1: The heading calls it a song for the Sabbath day, the weekly day of rest, when it was sung at the temple.
notes.96:1: Much of this psalm also appears in 1 Chronicles 16, sung when David brought the ark of the covenant (Israel's sacred chest) to Jerusalem.
notes.100:1: The heading calls it a psalm for giving thanks, probably sung as worshippers brought thank offerings into the temple courts.
notes.105:1: Its opening verses also appear in 1 Chronicles 16, in the song sung when the ark was brought to Jerusalem.
notes.106:1: It closes Book Four; its plea to be gathered from among the nations suggests it took shape when many Israelites were scattered in exile.
notes.107:1: Opening Book Five, it speaks of people gathered from every direction, which many link to the return from exile in Babylon.
notes.108:1: This psalm joins together parts of two earlier psalms, 57 and 60.
notes.110:1: Credited to David, it is a royal psalm, probably used when a new king was enthroned in Jerusalem.
notes.113:1: Psalms 113–118 form the 'Hallel' (praise), sung by Jewish families at Passover; Jesus and his disciples probably sang them at the Last Supper.
notes.118:1: The last of the Hallel psalms sung at Passover, it seems written for a thanksgiving procession entering the temple gates.
notes.119:1: The longest psalm: 22 stanzas of eight verses, every verse in a stanza starting with the same letter, working through the Hebrew alphabet.
notes.120:1: This opens the 'Songs of Ascents' (120–134), probably sung by pilgrims as they went up to Jerusalem for the yearly festivals.
notes.122:1: A pilgrim song credited to David, celebrating arrival at Jerusalem's gates after the festival journey.
notes.126:1: Most think it celebrates the return of exiles from Babylon after 538 BC, when the Persian king Cyrus allowed them home.
notes.127:1: The only Song of Ascents credited to Solomon, the king who built the temple.
notes.132:1: It recalls David's resolve to find a home for the ark, Israel's sacred chest, and may have been sung in temple processions.
notes.134:1: The last Song of Ascents, addressed to the Levites who kept watch and served in the temple through the night.
notes.136:1: Every line ends with the same refrain, likely sung responsively, with a leader singing and the congregation answering.
notes.137:1: It comes from the Jews taken to Babylon after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, recalling their time by Babylon's rivers, whether written there or soon after returning home.
notes.142:1: The heading links it to when David hid in a cave while fleeing King Saul.
notes.145:1: The last psalm credited to David, an acrostic whose verses run through the Hebrew alphabet.
notes.146:1: Psalms 146–150 form a closing group of praise, each beginning and ending with 'Hallelujah', meaning 'Praise the LORD'.
notes.147:1: Its mention of God rebuilding Jerusalem and gathering exiles suggests it comes from after the return from Babylon.
notes.150:1: The final psalm closes Book Five and the whole collection, naming many of the instruments used in temple worship.
